subject: English
chapter_title: The Wit that Won Hearts (Wit and Wisdom)
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 6 periods = 270 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 30min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.7): rectify five false statements about the story.
Let us discuss (p.8–9): answer questions on Golden Era, Tenali's place in court, and palace mood.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Court of Krishnadeva Raya Aloud

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the prose aloud (p.1–9) with students following in their textbooks; pause briefly at key moments — the king's wounded pride, the queen's appeal to Rama — to let the scene land.
Students work individually to rectify the five false statements from “Let us read” (p.7); teacher circulates and prompts with lines from the text where needed.

Class discusses three questions from “Let us discuss” (p.8–9): the Golden Era of Vijayanagara, Tenali Rama’s entry into court, and how the royal quarrel changed the palace atmosphere; students give textual evidence for each answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The opening of the story establishes the Vijayanagara Empire as a flourishing civilisation under Krishnadeva Raya — a warrior-poet king — before the domestic conflict with Thirumalambal unfolds; keep this dual frame clear during reading. A common difficulty is students conflating the queen’s yawning with deliberate disrespect; guide them back to the text’s phrase ‘involuntary human act’ when this confusion arises.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.7–8): discuss Extract 1 — queen’s appeal and Rama’s response.
Let us listen (p.13): fill in blanks selecting correct options after first listening.
Let us listen (p.13): number eight events in correct story order after second listening.

periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis and Listening to Rama’s Wit

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 (p.7–8) aloud; class discusses why the queen believes only Tenali Rama can help, what her regret reveals about her character, and how Rama’s measured response shows wisdom rather than haste.

Teacher reads the listening transcript aloud at a measured pace (p.46); students listen and fill in the two blanks — the thickness of the rope and the adjective used for the scholar — choosing from the given options (p.13).

Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students number the eight story events in the correct sequence (p.13), then pairs compare their ordering and resolve any differences before a brief whole-class check.

periods.teacher_notes: Extract 1 centres on the queen’s phrase ‘If I had known this would happen, I would have chosen another day’ — students often read this as complaint rather than regret; draw their attention to her tone of helplessness and her trust in Rama’s indirect approach. For the listening sequence task, remind students to anchor each event to a concrete detail in the transcript rather than guessing from story logic.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.13–14): mark and practise rising or falling intonation on ten questions.
Let us speak (p.14): ask and answer questions about a witty folktale character using correct intonation.

periods.activity_title: Rising and Falling: Practising Question Intonation

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains rising intonation for yes/no questions and falling intonation for wh- questions using two clear examples on the board; students mark the ten questions in “Let us speak” (p.13–14) individually before any oral work.

In pairs, students take turns saying each of the ten marked questions aloud with the correct intonation; teacher circulates, models corrections for persistent errors, and ensures quieter students lead at least one question.

Pairs choose a witty character from a folktale or story they know and take turns asking and answering the six prompt questions (p.14) — destination, purpose, transport, duration, companions, activities — using correct intonation throughout; two or three pairs share one exchange with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently use a falling tone on yes/no questions by habit; allow pairs to self-correct before the teacher intervenes, as peer correction in a guided-conversation format is more durable. The folktale exchange in the second activity invites students to bring characters from their own linguistic backgrounds — Akbar-Birbal, Vikramaditya, or regional trickster figures — which enriches the discussion.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.9–10): fill in ten blanks with appropriate sound words from the box.
Let us learn (p.10–11): match words to form compound words; fill blanks with compounds in context.
Let us learn (p.11–12): identify subordinate and main clauses; match conditional clause pairs.

periods.activity_title: Sound Words, Compound Words, and Conditionals

time_bands.activity: Students complete the ten-blank sound-word exercise (p.9–10) individually, choosing from the box; class reviews answers with the teacher explaining how each sound word creates atmosphere — ‘murmur’ for quiet tension, ‘roared’ for loud laughter.

Students match the eight word pairs to form compound words (p.10) and then use the compounds to fill the contextual blanks in the paragraph (p.11); teacher reviews closed, hyphenated, and open compound types with a quick board summary.

Teacher introduces the three types of conditional sentences using examples from the story text (p.11); students identify subordinate and main clauses in sentences 2 and 3, then match the six conditional clause pairs (p.12) individually before a whole-class check.

periods.teacher_notes: The three conditional types are encountered in authentic dialogue from the story — Rama’s ‘If you like, I will try my best’ and the queen’s ‘If I had known this would happen’ — anchoring grammar to familiar text reduces the abstraction. Students often blur the hypothetical past conditional with the impossible-past type; the clause-identification task on sentences 2 and 3 is the best corrective, so give it sufficient unhurried attention.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.9): complete the paragraph by choosing six idiomatic expressions from the box.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.15–16): plan and draft a narrative essay on teamwork or kindness.
Let us explore (p.16): read the sample limerick; compose an original limerick.

periods.activity_title: Narrative Essays and a Limerick of Their Own

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly walks through the narrative essay structure using ‘A Lesson in Responsibility’ as a shared reference (p.15): students call out which features — introduction, body with turning point, conclusion, first-person tone — they can see; teacher notes them on the board.

Students choose one of the two prompts (teamwork or kindness) and plan, draft, and revise a narrative essay in their notebooks; mid-way through drafting, a quick paired exchange lets each student hear one sentence of their partner’s opening and offer a single suggestion.

Teacher reads the limerick about Raju’s kite (p.16) aloud, pointing out the AABBA rhyme scheme and the comic twist in the final line; students then compose their own limerick on any topic, share with a neighbour, and one or two volunteers read theirs to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The narrative essay and the limerick are both forms that reward a personal voice — students who choose an experience they genuinely remember tend to write with more energy than those who invent a scenario, so encourage real memories for the essay prompts. The limerick’s constraint of the five-line AABBA scheme is itself a lesson in how form shapes expression, a thread that connects back to Tenali Rama’s own wit as a poet in the Ashtadiggajas.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.15–16): Draft, peer-respond, and revise narrative essay to completion.
Let us explore (p.16): Read sample limerick; compose an original limerick.

periods.activity_title: Wit, Words, and Wisdom: A Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Students draft their narrative essay in full (p.15–16) using the outline they formed — introduction, body with a turning point, and a conclusion that draws a lesson. Teacher circulates and gives brief individual feedback on structure and tone.

Structured peer response: each student exchanges their draft with a partner, who reads it and marks one strength and one suggestion using the feature checklist from "Let us write" (p.15). Writers then make one revision based on the feedback before the draft is considered complete.

Teacher introduces limericks from "Let us explore" (p.16): reads the sample aloud, pointing out the AABBA rhyme scheme and the twist in the last line — both echoes of the wit-and-surprise theme running through the chapter. Students compose their own limerick on any topic, share with the class, and the lesson closes with a brief reflection: what kind of intelligence does the chapter celebrate, and where have students seen it this term?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws the chapter together by completing the writing cycle — drafting, peer response, and revision — and then connecting the limerick's structural 'twist' to the wit-and-surprise logic that runs through the Tenali Rama stories. The peer-response step works best when students name a specific sentence they liked, not a vague 'it was good'; model this once before pairs begin. The library and chart-paper tasks in "Let us explore" (p.16) are excellent independent or home extensions for students who want to go further with the theme of wit across cultures.

items.source_lo: Student reads and interprets prose narrative by identifying character motivation, textual evidence, and cause-effect relationships using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Krishnadeva Raya’s court, the royal quarrel over yawning, and Tenali Rama’s indirect strategy to reconcile the king and queen.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best describes why King Krishnadeva Raya stopped speaking to Queen Thirumalambal?

options.label: A
options.text: The queen criticised the quality of his poem openly in the royal court.

options.label: B
options.text: The queen fell asleep while he was reciting his poem, which he saw as disrespect.

options.label: C
options.text: The queen refused to listen to his poem and walked out of the chamber.

options.label: D
options.text: The queen yawned repeatedly one tired evening as he recited his poem, and he interpreted it as disrespect.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student confused the queen’s private, involuntary act with a deliberate public insult.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student confused yawning with sleeping — a close but inaccurate reading of the text.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student invented a detail not present in the story; the queen remained present but yawned.

items.source_lo: Student reads and interprets prose narrative by identifying character motivation, textual evidence, and cause-effect relationships using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Krishnadeva Raya’s court, the royal quarrel over yawning, and Tenali Rama’s indirect strategy to reconcile the king and queen.
items.item_stem: In the story, Tenali Rama chooses to raise the topic of yawning through a discussion about paddy cultivation rather than by speaking to the king directly about the quarrel. In two to three sentences, explain why this indirect approach was more effective than a direct one would have been, using evidence from the king’s character and behaviour in the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The king was wounded by what he saw as disrespect and had allowed his pride to silence the queen entirely; a direct appeal would have met that same pride head-on and likely hardened his position. By engineering a natural, public yawn from the king himself during the paddy-seeds discussion, Rama made the king experience the very act he had condemned, allowing realisation to arrive without shame or confrontation.

items.source_context: Tenali Rama’s silk-wrapped bundle trick: a scholar’s challenge, tila-kashta-mahisha-bandhana, bundle of sticks, buffalo rope.
items.item_stem: Read the following statements about the story of Tenali Rama and the visiting scholar. Mark each statement True or False.

options.text: Tenali Rama arrived at the palace carrying a bundle wrapped in silk.
The court scholars welcomed the visiting scholar’s challenge with confidence.
The king burst out laughing when Rama explained what the bundle actually contained.
The visiting scholar had heard of tila-kashta-mahisha-bandhana but claimed not to have read it.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — the scholar had never heard of tila-kashta-mahisha-bandhana at all; he accepted defeat because the title was entirely unfamiliar to him.
2. True — the transcript states Rama arrived with a bundle wrapped in silk.
3. True — the transcript states the king burst out laughing at Rama’s explanation.
4. False — the court scholars were worried about defeat and the king’s anger, not confident.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a narrated story and demonstrates comprehension by selecting accurate details and sequencing events correctly using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tenali Rama’s silk-wrapped bundle trick: a scholar’s challenge, tila-kashta-mahisha-bandhana, bundle of sticks, buffalo rope.
items.item_stem: In the story of the visiting scholar, Tenali Rama reveals that tila-kashta-mahisha-bandhana is simply a bundle of sticks tied with a rope. In one to two sentences, explain what this moment reveals about how Rama uses language as a tool of wit.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Rama constructs an impressive-sounding Sanskrit compound from four ordinary words — sesame, stick, buffalo, and rope — to expose the scholar’s arrogance: a man who claimed mastery of thousands of works was defeated by a string of everyday nouns dressed up as a title. This shows that Rama’s wit lies in turning the scholar’s pride in language against him, using the very medium the scholar claimed to command.

items.source_context: Rising intonation for yes/no questions, falling intonation for wh- questions; discussing witty folktale characters.
items.item_stem:
Read the four questions below aloud to your partner, using the correct rising or falling intonation for each. Your partner will listen and give a thumbs-up when the intonation is correct.
(i) Did Tenali Rama tell the king about the quarrel directly?
(ii) What trick did Tenali Rama use in the royal court?
(iii) Is yawning a sign of disrespect?
(iv) Why did the king apologise to the queen?

expected_elements: Uses rising intonation on both yes/no questions (i) and (iii).
Uses falling intonation on both wh- questions (ii) and (iv).
Pronounces each question clearly enough for the partner to evaluate.
Corrects intonation on a second attempt when the partner signals an error.

items.source_context: Rising intonation for yes/no questions, falling intonation for wh- questions; discussing witty folktale characters.
items.item_stem: Think of a witty character from a folktale or story you know — someone like Tenali Rama, Birbal, or a similar figure from your own reading. Your partner will play someone who has never heard of this character. Conduct a short conversation in which you introduce the character, explain one clever thing they did, and share your opinion on why their kind of wit matters. Use at least two yes/no questions and two wh- questions during the exchange, with the correct intonation each time.

expected_elements: Names a specific witty character and states one clever act clearly.
Asks at least two yes/no questions with rising intonation.
Asks at least two wh- questions with falling intonation.
Offers a reasoned opinion on the value of the character’s wit.

items.item_stem: Write a short narrative essay (one introduction paragraph and one body paragraph only) based on the following situation: ‘A time when a small misunderstanding between two people was sorted out — not by arguing, but by a clever or kind act.’ Your introduction should set the scene and introduce the people involved. Your body paragraph should describe the misunderstanding and the clever or kind act that resolved it. Write in the first person.

expected_elements: Introduction sets scene and names the people involved clearly.
Body paragraph describes the misunderstanding with a specific detail.
A turning point — the clever or kind act — is clearly identified.
First-person voice is maintained throughout both paragraphs.

items.source_context: Narrative essay on teamwork or kindness: introduction, body with turning point, conclusion, first-person tone.
items.item_stem: In ‘The Wit that Won Hearts’, Tenali Rama resolves a conflict through an indirect, witty act rather than a direct conversation. Imagine you are Tenali Rama writing a personal journal entry that evening, reflecting on what happened and why you chose your particular approach. Write a complete narrative essay of three paragraphs — introduction, body, and conclusion — in the first person, using a personal and reflective tone throughout.

expected_elements: Adopts Tenali Rama’s voice convincingly with first-person perspective.
Body explains the paddy-seeds strategy and the reasoning behind it.
Reflects on the king’s pride as the obstacle requiring an indirect approach.
Conclusion conveys an insight or lesson drawn from the evening’s events.

items.item_stem: Match each compound word in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| quick-witted | speaking gently and quietly |
| soft-spoken | building or room where the royal court meets |
| courtroom | able to think and respond cleverly at speed |
| well-planned | bad-tempered and easily irritated |
| ill-tempered | carefully thought out in advance |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: quick-witted — able to think and respond cleverly at speed; soft-spoken — speaking gently and quietly; courtroom — building or room where the royal court meets; well-planned — carefully thought out in advance; ill-tempered — bad-tempered and easily irritated.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies vocabulary in context — sound words, compound words, and conditional sentence structures — using prose language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sound words (murmur, roared), compound words (quick-witted, soft-spoken), and three conditional types from the story’s dialogue.
items.item_stem:
The story contains three different types of conditional sentences. Read the three sentences below, drawn from the world of the story, and for each one: (a) name the conditional type (possible future, hypothetical, or impossible past), and (b) write one new sentence of your own using the same conditional structure but on a different topic.
1. If Tenali Rama is clever, he will find a way to help the queen.
2. If the king were less proud, he would listen to others more easily.
3. If the queen had not yawned that evening, the quarrel would never have begun.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sentence 1 is a possible future conditional (simple present + present modal); sentence 2 is a hypothetical conditional (simple past + past modal); sentence 3 is an impossible-past conditional (past perfect + would have + past participle). Students’ own sentences will vary; accept any sentence that uses the correct verb-tense pattern for each type.

items.source_context: Five-line AABBA limerick form with a twist in the final line; Raju’s kite and crow as the sample model.
items.item_stem:
Read the limerick below about Tenali Rama and answer the question that follows.

A courtier called Rama was sly,
His bundle of sticks caught the eye.
The scholar felt proud,
But froze in the crowd —
The ‘great work’ was rope, stick, and tie!

Identify the rhyme scheme of this limerick and explain the comic twist in the final line.

expected_elements: Correctly identifies the AABBA rhyme scheme with evidence from the limerick.
Explains that the comic twist deflates the scholar’s expectation of a grand work.
Notes the contrast between the impressive-sounding title and the ordinary objects.
Uses at least one full sentence that connects the twist to the theme of wit over pretension.

items.source_lo: Student creates an original limerick applying a fixed verse form and a comic twist using hands-on creative extension as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five-line AABBA limerick form with a twist in the final line; Raju’s kite and crow as the sample model.
items.item_stem: Write your own original limerick of five lines following the AABBA rhyme scheme. Your limerick must be set in the world of the Vijayanagara court — it may feature King Krishnadeva Raya, Tenali Rama, the queen, or any courtier — and must have a comic or surprising twist in the final line.

expected_elements: Limerick has exactly five lines with AABBA rhyme scheme.
At least one named character from the Vijayanagara court appears.
Final line delivers a clear comic or surprising twist.
Rhythm is roughly consistent across lines 1, 2, and 5 (longer) and 3, 4 (shorter).

result.section_coverage_note: Every section is covered; the closing sitting draws the chapter together in one synthesis.
